title: Date, occasion and translator
short: Pushkin's 'Prorok' (1826), written at Mikhailovskoe after news of the Decembrists' fate, published in Moskovskii vestnik (1828); Panin's literal version, 1888.
body: Pushkin wrote 'Prorok' ('The Prophet') in 1826, while still in exile on his family estate of Mikhailovskoe; it was first printed in the journal Moskovskii vestnik in 1828 (no. 3). The poem is usually connected with the crushing of the Decembrist rising of December 1825, the execution of five of its leaders in July 1826, and the exile of Pushkin's friends to Siberia; on the testimony of M. P. Pogodin, it was the first of four planned poems, of which the others are lost. Its subject is the call of the poet as prophet, told through biblical scenes of prophetic vocation. Ivan Panin translated it literally in his Poems by Alexander Pushkin (Boston, 1888), and his introduction reads its last lines as the poet's complete surrender of self-will.

title: thirst for the spirit
short: 'Духовной жаждою томим' ('tormented by spiritual thirst'): the psalmist's thirst for God in a dry land.
body: The first line sets the speaker in a state of spiritual longing, the condition for vocation. The image recalls the Psalms, as in Psalm 63:1 ('my soul thirsteth for thee ... in a dry and thirsty land') and Psalm 42:2, and Christ's blessing on those who 'hunger and thirst after righteousness' (Matthew 5:6). Pushkin's 'духовной жаждою' means spiritual thirst; Panin's 'thirst for the spirit' slightly changes the sense to a thirst whose object is the spirit. 'Томим' (tormented, wearied) also appears in Pushkin's love lyric 'Ya vas lyubil' (pushkin/41), where Panin renders it 'tormented' too.

title: sombre desert
short: 'В пустыне мрачной я влачился' ('in a gloomy desert I dragged myself along'): the wilderness where biblical prophets receive their call.
body: The desert (пустыня, wilderness) is the classic place of prophetic and ascetic preparation: Moses at the burning bush, Elijah at Horeb, John the Baptist, and Christ's temptation. Pushkin's 'мрачной' (gloomy, dark) colours it with despair, and 'влачился' (dragged myself along, trudged wearily) is a verb of exhaustion, which Panin keeps well with 'I was dragging myself'. The desert returns in line 25 ('Like a corpse I lay in the desert'), framing the transformation.

title: six-winged seraph
greek: Hebrew seraphim (burning ones); Russian шестикрылый серафим
short: 'Шестикрылый серафим': from Isaiah 6:2, where seraphim with six wings stand above the throne of God at Isaiah's call.
body: In Isaiah 6, the prophet sees the Lord enthroned, with seraphim above him: 'each one had six wings; with twain he covered his face, and with twain he covered his feet, and with twain he did fly' (6:2). One seraph flies to Isaiah with a live coal from the altar and touches his lips, purging his sin (6:6-7), and Isaiah then accepts his mission. Pushkin keeps the seraph and the purifying fire but greatly expands the violence of the transformation. Commentators have long tied the poem to Isaiah's call. A late memoir attributed to A. O. Smirnova-Rosset, of uncertain reliability, instead links its origin with a reading of Ezekiel.

title: the parting of the roads
short: 'На перепутье': at a crossroads, the place of choice; Panin's phrase echoes the KJV's 'parting of the way' (Ezekiel 21:21).
body: 'Перепутье' means a crossroads or fork in the road, a traditional place of decision and of supernatural encounter in Russian folklore. The seraph appears to the speaker at the moment when he must choose a path. Panin's 'parting of the roads' recalls the King James phrase in Ezekiel 21:21, where the king of Babylon 'stood at the parting of the way, at the head of the two ways, to use divination'; it is an apt choice in a poem saturated with prophetic language. The image also anticipates the end: the prophet will be sent 'over land and sea', having taken the road of vocation.

anchor: fingers as light as a dream
title: With fingers as light as a dream
short: 'Перстами лёгкими как сон': 'персты' is the Church Slavonic word for fingers, a sign of the poem's elevated biblical register.
body: The seraph's first touch is gentle, light as sleep or a dream ('сон' means both). 'Персты' (fingers) is the Slavonic form, replacing the everyday Russian 'пальцы'; Pushkin uses such words throughout ('зеницы' for eyes, 'уста' for lips, 'десница' for right hand, 'глагол' for word) to give the poem the sound of the Russian Bible and liturgy. The gentleness of these first transformations, eyes and ears, contrasts sharply with the violence that follows at the mouth and heart. Panin's 'as light as a dream' is exact.

title: Like the eyes of a frightened eagle
short: 'Отверзлись вещие зеницы, / Как у испуганной орлицы': the prophetic pupils opened like those of a startled she-eagle.
body: The opened eyes are 'вещие', prophetic, seeing what is hidden, and 'зеницы' (pupils, eyes) is again Slavonic. 'Отверзлись' (were opened) recalls the biblical opening of eyes, as in the healing of the blind. The simile of the eagle, proverbially keen-sighted, adds the startled wide-eyed look of a creature roused. Pushkin's 'орлица' is feminine, a she-eagle; Panin's 'eagle' loses the gender, which some readers associate with the protective mother eagle of Deuteronomy 32:11. Panin's 'opened wise' is his attempt at 'вещие' (prophetic, knowing).

title: The cosmos heard
short: With transformed hearing, the prophet perceives the whole universe from top to bottom: the heavens, angels, sea-creatures and growing vines.
body: Lines 11-14 form a vertical catalogue of creation: 'И внял я неба содроганье, / И горний ангелов полёт, / И гад морских подводный ход, / И дольней лозы прозябанье' ('and I heard the shuddering of the sky, and the angels' flight on high, and the underwater course of sea creatures, and the growth of the vine in the valley'). The range runs from the heavens, through the angels and the depths of the sea, to the plant world on earth, so the prophet's hearing embraces the whole created order. 'Горний' (on high, celestial) and 'дольний' (of the vale, earthly) are paired Slavonic opposites. Panin's 'And ... And ... And' keeps the biblical parataxis of the Russian.

title: the polyps in the sea
short: Pushkin's 'гад морских подводный ход', 'the underwater movement of sea creatures'; 'гады' means reptiles or creeping things in general, not polyps.
body: The Russian 'гад' (plural 'гады') is the Slavonic word for creeping things, reptiles and similar creatures, the word used in the Russian Bible for the 'creeping things' of Genesis 1. 'Гады морские' are therefore creatures of the sea in general, perhaps recalling Psalm 104:25 ('this great and wide sea, wherein are things creeping innumerable'). Panin's 'polyps' is oddly specific and introduces a zoological term; his 'creeping' is closer to the word's root sense, but 'ход' means movement or progress, not specifically creeping. The line's point is that the prophet hears what is normally inaudible and hidden, motion in the depths of the sea.

anchor: out he tore my sinful tongue
title: out he tore my sinful tongue
short: 'И вырвал грешный мой язык, / И празднословный и лукавый': the seraph tears out the sinful, idle and deceitful tongue, a violent version of Isaiah's purified lips.
body: In Isaiah 6:5 the prophet cries that he is 'a man of unclean lips', and the seraph's coal purges them. Pushkin's seraph does far more: he seizes the lips ('приник ко мне к устам') and tears out the tongue. 'Празднословный' (idle-speaking) recalls Christ's warning about 'every idle word' (Matthew 12:36) and the Lenten prayer of St Ephrem, familiar in Orthodox liturgy, which asks to be spared 'the spirit of idle talk'. 'Лукавый' means crafty, deceitful. Panin's 'empty and false speech' is a fair paraphrase of both adjectives. The scene shows that the poet's old, worldly speech must be destroyed before prophetic speech is possible.

anchor: the fang of the wise serpent
title: the fang of the wise serpent
short: 'И жало мудрыя змеи / В уста замершие мои / Вложил десницею кровавой': the wise serpent's sting, placed with a bloody right hand; it echoes 'wise as serpents' (Matthew 10:16).
body: The new tongue is 'жало мудрыя змеи', the sting of the wise serpent. The archaic genitive 'мудрыя' (for modern 'мудрой') is Church Slavonic. The serpent here is not the tempter of Genesis but the wisdom of Matthew 10:16, 'be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves', words spoken to apostles being sent into a hostile world. A forked serpent's tongue was popularly believed to be its sting ('жало'), so the image makes the prophet's speech both wise and piercing. Panin's 'fang' is inaccurate; 'sting' is standard. 'Десница' (right hand) and 'кровавой' (bloody) stress the violence.

title: a coal with flaming blaze
short: Isaiah's live coal touched the lips (6:6-7); Pushkin's seraph cuts open the breast and puts a burning coal in place of the heart.
body: Pushkin transforms the source decisively: 'И он мне грудь рассек мечом, / И сердце трепетное вынул, / И угль, пылающий огнём, / Во грудь отверстую водвинул' ('and he cut open my breast with a sword, and took out my trembling heart, and pushed a coal blazing with fire into the opened breast'). In Isaiah the coal purges lips; here it replaces the human heart altogether, a fusion with Ezekiel's promise of a 'new heart' (Ezekiel 36:26). 'Угль' is the Slavonic form of 'уголь' (coal). The trembling heart of human feeling becomes a fire, so the prophet will burn others' hearts in turn (last line).

title: Like a corpse I lay
greek: Как труп в пустыне я лежал
short: 'Как труп в пустыне я лежал': the deathlike collapse of the visionary, as in Ezekiel and Revelation; the old self has died.
body: After the operation, the speaker lies like a corpse in the desert. Biblical visionaries often fall as dead before the divine: Ezekiel falls on his face (Ezekiel 1:28) and John 'fell at his feet as dead' (Revelation 1:17). The line is also a death and rebirth: the man with ordinary eyes, ears, tongue and heart is dead, and only God's voice can raise the prophet. It is the poem's only short, self-contained sentence of stillness between the violent operations and the commanding voice. Panin translates it exactly.

title: Arise, O prophet, and listen, and guide
greek: Восстань, пророк, и виждь, и внемли
short: Pushkin's 'Восстань, пророк, и виждь, и внемли': 'arise, prophet, and see, and hearken'. Panin's 'and guide' is not in the Russian.
body: God's command echoes Ezekiel 2:1 ('Son of man, stand upon thy feet, and I will speak unto thee'). The Russian imperatives are in Church Slavonic form: 'восстань' (arise), 'виждь' (see), 'внемли' (hearken, attend), corresponding to the two senses the seraph transformed, sight and hearing. Panin renders 'внемли' as 'listen' but gives 'guide' where Pushkin has 'виждь' (see), which breaks the link with the opened eyes of lines 6-8 and may result from a misreading. Students relying on Panin should note the error, since 'see and hear' sums up the prophet's new perception before the mission of the final lines.

anchor: Be thou filled with my will
title: Be thou filled with my will
short: 'Исполнись волею моей': the prophet is to be filled with God's will; Panin's introduction reads this as the poet's surrender of self-will.
body: The verb 'исполнись' (be filled, be fulfilled) can also mean 'carry out', so the line suggests both possession by divine will and its execution. Panin, in the introduction to his 1888 translation, treats this line as the climax of Pushkin's spiritual development, an ideal that ended, as he puts it, in the 'complete surrender of self-will'. Other readers stress the political context of 1826: after the Decembrists' defeat, the poet claims an authority higher than any tsar's. These readings are not exclusive, and the poem's power derives partly from its ambiguity between religious vocation and the Romantic idea of the poet as prophet.

title: Fire with the word the hearts of men
short: 'Глаголом жги сердца людей': 'burn the hearts of people with the word'; 'глагол' is the Slavonic word for speech or word.
body: The famous last line joins the new heart of fire to the new speech of the serpent's sting: the prophet is to burn men's hearts with his word. 'Глагол' in modern Russian means 'verb', but in Church Slavonic it means word or utterance, especially divine utterance, so the line has a scriptural ring. Compare Jeremiah 23:29, 'Is not my word like as a fire? saith the Lord', and Jeremiah 20:9, where God's word is 'as a burning fire shut up in my bones'. The line became a watchword of the Russian idea of the poet's mission, and Lermontov answered it with his own bitter 'Prorok' (1841), in which the prophet is stoned and mocked.

title: Form and Slavonic diction
short: Thirty lines of iambic tetrameter in a single stanza, dense with Church Slavonic words; Panin renders it into unrhymed English with biblical 'And'.
body: 'Prorok' is a single paragraph of thirty lines of iambic tetrameter, with varied rhyme, so it moves without stanza breaks from desert to command. Its diction is deliberately archaic and scriptural: Slavonic forms such as 'персты', 'зеницы', 'уста', 'десница', 'угль', 'глагол' and the genitive 'мудрыя'. The many lines beginning 'И' (and) imitate biblical parataxis. Panin preserves this with his repeated 'And' and archaic 'mine eyes', but without metre and rhyme the English cannot convey the poem's cumulative, hammering rhythm. The poem was set to music by Rimsky-Korsakov among others.

title: Isaiah or Ezekiel?
short: The poem combines Isaiah 6 (seraph, coal) with Ezekiel's vision and call (Ezekiel 1-3), including the prophet who lies prostrate before the voice of God.
body: Though contemporaries associated the poem with Isaiah, the structure follows a pattern found in Ezekiel: a vision, the prophet falling down, a voice commanding him to stand, and a mission to an obstinate people (Ezekiel 1:28-3:11). In Ezekiel 3:1-3 the prophet even eats the scroll that God gives him, an incorporation of the divine word comparable to Pushkin's new tongue and heart. A late memoir attributed to A. O. Smirnova-Rosset, of uncertain reliability, links the poem's origin with a reading of Ezekiel, while most commentary stresses Isaiah. Many readers see Pushkin as fusing several prophetic call narratives into a new myth of the poet.
